  title:            mönstrad filtmatta, intarsia, shyrdak
  description:      Fryst hösten 1999, efter att ett par ullföremål i samlingen angripits av klädesmal. | Mönstrad matta tillverkad av filt i en teknik som kallas intarsia.
Färger: rött, grönt, blåt och svart och vitt .
Konturlinjer sydda med 2 trådar, en S och en Z tvinnad. Dessa knturer är en del av knstruktionen då de två färgdelarna sys samman.
Mattor av denna typ är tillverkade av 2 lager filt. Överst det mönstrade i olika färger, då detta är sytt kviltas de samman med en hel filt av svart eller brun ull för att stabilisera hela mattan.
Kanter: Denna typ av mattor är tillskurna och därför kantade med i detta
  location on file: Sweden  (held by: Museum of World Culture)

  title:            Head of a Follower of Shiva
  description:      Khmer patrons and artists produced works of art that could depict either a deified king or a god who has royal attributes. The Khmer cult of the god-king allowed for such fluidity of interpretation. Presence of a third eye in the forehead and matted locks of hair are attributes both of the Hindu god Shiva and the followers who emulated him in order to get closer to him.
  location on file: Cambodia, Angkor, 10th century  (held by: Cleveland Museum of Art)

THE HOLDING MUSEUM'S METADATA
  title:            Head of a Deity or a Deified King
  description:      The diadem is depicted tied to the intricate tiered headdress worn only by a god or king. Without further attributes, the identity cannot be known. Khmer sculptors of the 10th century emphasized powerful forms and extroverted expressions. The incised pupils suggest that this sculpture underwent the ritual of awakening, in which the eyes were added last. The royal head on the left is from a temple dedicated to Shiva, which was established by the Khmer king Jayavarman IV (928–942) in his remote capital of Koh Ker, 100 miles north of Angkor.
  location on file: Cambodia, Koh Ker, Reign of Jayavarman IV, 928-941  (held by: Cleveland Museum of Art)

THE HOLDING MUSEUM'S METADATA
  title:            Slendang (Shoulder Cloth)
  description:      Chinese people living in the coastal cities of northern Java made and traded silk batiks like this one. The silk was imported from China, and the motifs were always Chinese. The "luk wan" bird, a variation of the Chinese phoenix that occurs on this shoulder cloth, was one of the most common motifs on silk batiks, as is the greenish color of the background. The striped border was meant to simulate fringe even though each end is actually finished with fringe. Silk batiks were made for export, particularly to Bali where they were worn at festivals by wealthy people.
  location on file: Indonesia, Java, North Coast, 19th - early 20th century  (held by: Cleveland Museum of Art)

THE HOLDING MUSEUM'S METADATA
  title:            Sarong
  description:      Batiks made along the northern coast of Java were influenced not only by Chinese motifs and designs but also European, as a result of the Dutch presence in Indonesia from the sixteenth to the twentieth centuries. In this sarong, European influence is clearly evident in the sprays of flowers and types of birds represented. Batiks dyed only in indigo were a specialty of Indramaju. Shading and contrast are skillfully achieved through different intensities of blue, through the character and thickness of line, and by the use of tiny dots.

  title:            Longyi
  description:      Woman's longyi made of silk with a floating weft weave. It consists of a tube made up of a warp length of cloth sewn by hand across a weft seam, so that the warp runs horizontally around the body of the wearer. Dark red ground with weft yellow acheik (horizontal wave) patterns in 'joe gee jay' style ('jay' means hook or line). THIS RECORD CLAIMS TO BE ethnicity : Filipino (Philippines) category : textile THE HOLDING MUSEUM'S METADATA title: Mandaya ikat textile (dagmay) description: This textile is a Mandaya abacá ikat cloth woven in southeastern Mindanao. THE HOLDING MUSEUM'S METADATA
  title:            Single Leaf from a Gospel Book with a  Portrait of Saint Luke
  description:      Christianity arrived in Ethiopia during the 300s CE, well before reaching northern Europe. Typical of panel and manuscript painting in Ethiopia, this leaf is decorated with bright colors and a joyous interplay of geometric pattern. The full-page miniature depicts the evangelist Luke, with his symbol, the ox, within the arch above. The short text is in the Ge‘ez (the centuries-old church language of Ethiopian Orthodoxy) and consists of the opening lines of the gospel of Luke: “Make this image of St. Luke with this bull––his prayer (offering)––and with his blessings, they were with us. Amen.”
  location on file: Empire of Ethiopia, Tigray region (Ethiopia)  (held by: Cleveland Museum of Art)
